title: What drug and alcohol training does the FAA require under 14 CFR Part 120?
seoTitle: FAA Part 120 drug and alcohol training
description: 14 CFR Part 120 training explained: EAP education and employee training, 60 minute supervisor modules, recurrent supervisor training and record retention.
shortAnswer: Under 14 CFR Part 120, FAA regulated aviation employers must run an Employee Assistance Program with drug education and initial training for safety sensitive employees, give supervisors who make reasonable cause drug testing decisions at least 60 minutes of initial training plus a reasonable recurrent program, and give supervisors who make alcohol reasonable suspicion decisions at least 60 minutes on alcohol indicators. Employees must also receive written alcohol education materials covering the topics listed in 14 CFR 120.223.
keyTakeaways: 14 CFR 120.115 requires an EAP with education (informational material, a hotline number and the drug policy) and initial employee training on the effects of drug use and the behavioral cues that may indicate it.
Supervisors who make reasonable cause drug determinations need at least 60 minutes of initial training and a reasonable recurrent training program in later years (14 CFR 120.115(c)(3) and (4)).
Supervisors who decide on alcohol reasonable suspicion tests need at least 60 minutes on physical, behavioral, speech and performance indicators of alcohol misuse (14 CFR 120.223(b)).
A reasonable cause drug test needs at least two supervisors to concur, one trained in detecting drug use symptoms, except at small non Part 121 employers (14 CFR 120.109(d)).
From December 20, 2027, Part 120 extends to Part 145 repair stations outside the United States that perform safety sensitive maintenance on Part 121 aircraft, unless recognized under 120.10.
regulator: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Office of Aerospace Medicine, Drug Abatement Division, under 14 CFR Part 120 and the U.S. Department of Transportation procedures in 49 CFR Part 40
appliesTo: Part 119 certificate holders operating under Part 121 or Part 135, and operators defined in 14 CFR 91.147
Air traffic control facilities not operated by the FAA or the U.S. military
Part 145 repair stations and contractors that elect, or from December 20, 2027 in some cases are required, to run a Part 120 program
Employees performing the nine safety sensitive functions in 14 CFR 120.105 and 120.215, and their supervisors

sections.heading: Which aviation employers and employees does Part 120 cover?

blocks.text: Part 120 covers Part 121 and Part 135 operators, 91.147 air tour operators, non-FAA air traffic control facilities and every individual who performs a listed safety sensitive function for them, directly or by contract at any tier. [14 CFR 120.1](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/120.1) sets the applicability.

The safety sensitive functions in 14 CFR 120.105 (drug testing) and 120.215 (alcohol testing) are the same nine duties, and they include assistants, helpers and people in training status, whether full time, part time, temporary or intermittent:

items: Flight crewmember, flight attendant and flight instruction duties.
Aircraft dispatcher and operations control specialist duties.
Aircraft maintenance and preventive maintenance duties.
Ground security coordinator and aviation screening duties.

blocks.title: Transition: foreign repair stations
blocks.text: An amendment published on December 18, 2024 added 120.1(d). Beginning December 20, 2027, Part 145 certificate holders outside the United States that perform safety sensitive maintenance on Part 121 air carrier aircraft fall under Part 120, unless they have obtained recognition under 120.10. As at November 2026 this obligation has not yet commenced, but training programs for those repair stations need to be ready before that date.

sections.heading: What must the Employee Assistance Program education include?

blocks.text: Every Part 120 employer must provide an Employee Assistance Program (EAP), in house or contracted, that includes drug education for employees. [14 CFR 120.115(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-120.115) sets three minimum education elements:

items: Display and distribution of informational material.
Display and distribution of a community service hotline telephone number for employee assistance.
Display and distribution of the employer's policy on drug use in the workplace.

blocks.text: The policy must explain the consequences under the rule of using drugs while performing safety sensitive functions, of a verified positive drug test result, and of refusing a required test. Education here means making information available; it is distinct from the training obligations below, and Part 120 sets no minimum duration for it.

sections.heading: What drug training must safety sensitive employees receive?

blocks.text: Employers must implement "a reasonable program of initial training for employees" under 14 CFR 120.115(c)(1). The training must cover at least the effects and consequences of drug use on individual health, safety and the work environment, and the manifestations and behavioral cues that may indicate drug use and abuse.

Unlike the transit rule in [FTA drug and alcohol training requirements](/regulations/fta-drug-and-alcohol-training-requirements), the FAA sets no minimum number of minutes for employee training. The employer must document all training given and identify the employee and supervisor EAP training in its drug testing program, which is the evidence an FAA Drug Abatement inspector will ask to see.

sections.heading: What training do supervisors need for reasonable cause and reasonable suspicion testing?

blocks.text: Supervisors need two separate 60 minute modules, one on drug use indicators and one on alcohol misuse indicators, and the drug module must be refreshed through a recurrent program. The two requirements come from different subparts of Part 120.

blocks.text: The testing rule shows why the training matters. Under 14 CFR 120.109(d), a reasonable cause drug test must rest on "a reasonable and articulable belief" based on specific contemporaneous indicators, and at least two supervisors, one of whom is trained in detecting the symptoms of possible drug use, must substantiate and concur in the decision. An employer other than a Part 121 certificate holder with 50 or fewer safety sensitive employees may rely on one trained supervisor.

The recurrent drug training requirement is a key difference from the motor carrier rule described in [DOT drug and alcohol supervisor training](/regulations/dot-drug-and-alcohol-supervisor-training), where recurrent supervisor training is expressly not required. Part 120 does not define "reasonable", so the employer should document its chosen interval and rationale.

sections.heading: What alcohol education materials must employees receive?

blocks.text: Employers must distribute written materials explaining the alcohol testing requirements and their own policies to every covered employee before alcohol testing starts and to anyone later hired or transferred into a covered position. They must also give written notice to employee organization representatives that the information is available.

items: The person designated to answer employee questions about the materials.
The categories of employees covered and the period of the work day when they must comply.
Prohibited conduct, the circumstances of testing, the testing procedures and what counts as a refusal.
Consequences of a violation, including immediate removal from safety sensitive functions and the return to duty process in 49 CFR Part 40, Subpart O.
Consequences of an alcohol concentration of 0.02 or greater but less than 0.04.
The effects of alcohol misuse on health, work and personal life, signs of an alcohol problem, ways to resolve it, and intervening when a problem is suspected.

blocks.text: Any employer policy that goes further than Part 120 may be included but must be "clearly and obviously described as being based on independent authority."

blocks.text: Under 14 CFR 120.219, alcohol program training records, including alcohol awareness materials, documentation of supervisor reasonable suspicion training and certification that training complies with the rule, must be kept for two years. For organizing these files see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry separates the drug indicators, alcohol indicators, two supervisor concurrence rule and documentation steps into distinct knowledge points with their own assessment items. An employer can then show which competencies each designated supervisor demonstrated at initial and recurrent training, rather than only that 60 minutes were logged.

faqs.q: How often must FAA reasonable cause supervisor training be repeated?
faqs.a: 14 CFR 120.115(c)(4) requires a reasonable recurrent training program for supervisors making reasonable cause drug determinations in subsequent years, without fixing an interval. Many employers choose an annual cycle, but whatever interval is chosen should be written into the drug testing program with a rationale.

faqs.q: Can one 120 minute course satisfy both supervisor requirements?
faqs.a: Yes, if the records show at least 60 minutes on drug use indicators under 120.115 and at least 60 minutes on alcohol misuse indicators under 120.223(b). A single combined completion record that does not show the split leaves the employer unable to prove that each minimum was met.

faqs.q: Do flight attendants and mechanics need Part 120 training?
faqs.a: Yes. Flight attendant duties and aircraft maintenance and preventive maintenance duties are safety sensitive functions under 14 CFR 120.105 and 120.215, so those employees receive EAP education, initial drug training and alcohol education materials, including contractors at any tier.

faqs.q: What happens when a certificated airman refuses a test?
faqs.a: The employer must notify the FAA within 2 working days when a covered employee holding a Part 61, 63 or 65 certificate refuses a required drug test (120.111(d)) or alcohol test (120.221(d)). Supervisors and program managers should be trained on this reporting step.
